adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — Worker exceptions are marked complete so the commit loop permanently advances past failed results.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method in queue_consumer.py lines 127-152, when an exception occurs during result_processor execution (caught at line 145), the code falls through to the finally block (lines 147-152) which calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset). This marks the offset as complete even though processing failed. The commit loop in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop() (lines 262-280) will then commit these offsets, permanently advancing past failed messages. This means failed messages are lost and won't be reprocessed. The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling at line 1893 actually verifies this behavior - it expects no commits when processing fails, but the current implementation would mark offsets complete anyway.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — The error-path test can pass before the one-second commit loop runs even though the failed offset is later committed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line 1922, it asserts `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` after processing two messages where the first one fails. However, examining the `_commit_loop` in `queue_consumer.py` (lines 268-287), it runs every 1 second (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`). The test waits up to 2 seconds (20 iterations * 0.1s) for processing to complete, but the assertion happens immediately after. The issue is that even when processing fails (line 145-148 in queue_consumer.py), the offset is still marked complete via the `finally` block (lines 149-157). So both offsets 100 and 101 would be marked complete, and when the commit loop runs, it would commit offset 101. The test's assertion that no commits happen is flawed - it depends on timing whether the 1-second commit loop has run yet. This is a real test bug where the test can pass spuriously.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148 — Worker exceptions still mark the offset complete, so a failed result is committed and permanently dropped.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method in queue_consumer.py lines 119-147, the code has a try/except/finally block where exceptions during result_processor() are caught and logged (line 141-143), but the finally block (lines 144-147) always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(). This means even when processing fails with an exception, the offset is marked complete and will be committed. The test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling test at line 1858 confirms this is problematic behavior - it expects that after an error, offsets should NOT be committed, but the current implementation will commit them anyway since complete_offset is called in finally.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:231 — Shutdown sets every worker's exit flag before draining queued work and stops the commit loop first, so pending messages are abandoned without a final commit.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown sequence in FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (lines 231-243), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown() on queues, then joins workers. In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (lines 335-338), it sets shutdown_event which stops the commit loop, then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). The issue is that when workers have their shutdown flag set, they will exit their run loop after processing the current item, but items still in the queue may not be processed. More critically, the commit thread is stopped before ensuring all pending work is committed - the shutdown_event.set() stops the commit loop, and then queue_pool.shutdown() is called. Any offsets that were completed but not yet committed in the 1-second commit interval will be lost. This is a real data loss/correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — WorkItem retains an unused Message field, needlessly coupling the queue abstraction and all its tests to Arroyo message construction.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the `message` field in WorkItem is 'unused' and creates unnecessary coupling. However, looking at the diff, the WorkItem dataclass is defined with a `message` field that stores the original Kafka message. While the current implementation may not use this field extensively in the shown code paths, retaining the original message is a reasonable design choice for debugging, logging, or future extensions. The field is not 'needlessly' coupling anything - it's part of the data structure design. The tests do construct WorkItems with messages, but this is appropriate for testing the actual implementation. This is at most a minor design opinion, not a verifiable defect or important issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:144 — Worker exceptions are acknowledged as complete, so the commit loop advances past failed Kafka messages without retrying them.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in queue_consumer.py lines 130-147, the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method catches all exceptions in the try block but still calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` in the finally block regardless of whether processing succeeded or failed. This means when an exception occurs during `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)`, the offset is still marked as complete, allowing the commit loop to advance past failed messages without any retry mechanism. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` at line 1858 even demonstrates this behavior - it expects that after an exception, no commits happen, but the actual implementation will mark the offset complete anyway.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:317 — Submission/decode/grouping failures are marked complete, allowing malformed transient failures to be committed and permanently dropped.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 305-320 in queue_consumer.py, when an exception occurs during message submission (decode/grouping), the code catches the exception, logs it, and then marks the offset as both added and completed. This means if a transient failure occurs (e.g., temporary network issue during decode), the message will be marked as processed and its offset will be committed, causing the message to be permanently lost. The code at lines 314-319 shows: `except Exception: logger.exception(...) if isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue): self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.add_offset(...) self.queue_pool.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. This is a real bug - transient failures should not result in the message being committed as processed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:231 — Shutdown signals workers to exit before draining queued work, so a graceful stop abandons outstanding messages and replays them after restart.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown() method in FixedQueuePool (lines 231-243), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) on all queues, then joins workers. The OrderedQueueWorker.run() method (lines 117-143) checks self.shutdown at the start of each loop iteration. When shutdown is True, the worker will exit after processing the current item, but any items still in the queue won't be processed. The queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is called after setting the shutdown flag, so workers may exit before the queue is fully drained. This means outstanding messages in the queues will be abandoned and replayed after restart, which is a correctness issue for a message processing system.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — The processor-failure test permits no commit before the one-second commit loop runs, so it misses failed work being acknowledged and committed.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 1922 (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling) checks that when processing fails, offsets are not committed. However, looking at the implementation in queue_consumer.py, the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block (lines 139-140), meaning even failed work items get their offsets marked as complete. The test assertion 'assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets' may pass only because the 1-second commit loop hasn't run yet, not because the error handling is correct. This is a legitimate test design concern - the test doesn't properly verify the intended behavior around error handling and offset commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:314 — The claimed cross-group concurrency test only counts completions and never proves separate queues overlap, so serial execution still passes.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test `test_concurrent_processing_different_groups` at line 314, it submits 4 items to different groups and waits for all to complete, then asserts `len(self.processed_results) == 4`. The test only verifies that all items were processed, not that they were processed concurrently. The test name claims to verify concurrent processing across groups, but serial execution would also pass this test. This is a valid concern about test coverage - the test doesn't actually prove concurrency (e.g., by checking timing overlap or using synchronization primitives to verify parallel execution). However, this is a test quality issue, not a bug in the production code.
